Serologic testing for antiviral antibodies Recent encephalitis and radial chorioretinal lesions without leakage on FA are consistent with WNV. WNV IgG and IgM tests were positive. Rheumatoid factor, which can cause false-positive WNV serology, was negative. The differential diagnosis for multifocal chorioretinitis includes nonhelminthic infectious causes, such as presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (POHS), and infectious causes, such as syphilis, tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis, pneumocystis choroiditis, and WNV. Although vitritis makes POHS much less likely, 5% of POHS patients, as a subset of multifocal choroiditis, have a linear streak of histoplasmosis spots parallel to the equator (ie, Schlaegel lines). Ocular toxoplasmosis classically presents with vitritis overlying focal retinitis (ie, a headlight in the fog). Active toxoplasmosis is unlikely without retinitis (choice A). The remaining etiologies are unlikely with negative serology and inconsistent imaging. Helminthic infections can cause chorioretinitis. However, typically there are also anterior segment findings, like keratitis or iridocyclitis in onchocerciasis. Ocular cysticercosis can cause intracranial calcifications. Toxocara and other nematodes can cause subretinal tracks with diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis (DUSN), consistent with linear chorioretinal lesions. However, serologic and stool studies and peripheral blood smears are of little utility in helminthic infections (choice B).1Stool ova and parasite testing is low yield for toxocara, because ingested eggs cause an eosinophilic granulomatous immune reaction incompatible with helminth survival.2Although multiple toxocariasis phenotypes have been described, including DUSN and diffuse chorioretinal inflammation, the most common presentation is unilateral pediatric subretinal peripheral or posterior pole granulomas with clear media. Adult ocular toxocariasis is exceedingly rare and usually presents with vitritis overlying a hazy white granuloma.3 Noninfectious causes include sarcoidosis, punctate inner choroidopathy, birdshot retinochoroidopathy, idiopathic multifocal choroiditis, and multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis. Linear periphlebitis and inflammatory aggregates in the vitreous, described as a string of pearls, can be seen in sarcoidosis. The other autoimmune etiologies are diagnoses of exclusion. Infection should be ruled out before treating empirically with corticosteroids (choice C). WNV, detected with serologic testing for antiviral antibodies (choice D), is a single-stranded RNA flavivirus transmitted byCulexgenus mosquitoes. Approximately 70% to 80% of human WNV infections are subclinical. Most symptomatic cases present with acute fever, headache, weakness, myalgia, arthralgia, gastrointestinal upset, and/or transient maculopapular rash. Less than 1% of cases exhibit neuroinvasive disease. The most common ocular complication is multifocal chorioretinitis, but cranial nerve palsy, nystagmus, optic neuritis, retinal vasculitis, and anterior uveitis have been reported. Age greater than 45 years and diabetes are risk factors for WNV chorioretinitis.4 In neuroinvasive disease, CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis. However, neutrophils predominate early, are rapidly recruited to the site of WNV infection in mice, and support viral replication.5 MRI may show abnormalities in the basal ganglia, thalamus, and brainstem in patients with encephalitis. Fundus photos and retina OCT typically show a linear chorioretinitis due to spread along the retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL).6WNV can spread hematogenously via the choroid or neurally from the central nervous system to the RNFL, which may explain the combination of scattered and linear lesion formations in this patient. The patient’s symptoms and vitritis resolved with observation, while chorioretinal lesions persisted (Figure 2).

Serologic testing for antiviral antibodies Recent encephalitis and radial chorioretinal lesions without leakage on FA are consistent with WNV. WNV IgG and IgM tests were positive. Rheumatoid factor, which can cause false-positive WNV serology, was negative. The differential diagnosis for multifocal chorioretinitis includes nonhelminthic infectious causes, such as presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (POHS), and infectious causes, such as syphilis, tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis, pneumocystis choroiditis, and WNV. Although vitritis makes POHS much less likely, 5% of POHS patients, as a subset of multifocal choroiditis, have a linear streak of histoplasmosis spots parallel to the equator (ie, Schlaegel lines). Ocular toxoplasmosis classically presents with vitritis overlying focal retinitis (ie, a headlight in the fog). Active toxoplasmosis is unlikely without retinitis (choice A). The remaining etiologies are unlikely with negative serology and inconsistent imaging. Helminthic infections can cause chorioretinitis. However, typically there are also anterior segment findings, like keratitis or iridocyclitis in onchocerciasis. Ocular cysticercosis can cause intracranial calcifications. Toxocara and other nematodes can cause subretinal tracks with diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis (DUSN), consistent with linear chorioretinal lesions. However, serologic and stool studies and peripheral blood smears are of little utility in helminthic infections (choice B).1Stool ova and parasite testing is low yield for toxocara, because ingested eggs cause an eosinophilic granulomatous immune reaction incompatible with helminth survival.2Although multiple toxocariasis phenotypes have been described, including DUSN and diffuse chorioretinal inflammation, the most common presentation is unilateral pediatric subretinal peripheral or posterior pole granulomas with clear media. Adult ocular toxocariasis is exceedingly rare and usually presents with vitritis overlying a hazy white granuloma.3 Noninfectious causes include sarcoidosis, punctate inner choroidopathy, birdshot retinochoroidopathy, idiopathic multifocal choroiditis, and multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis. Linear periphlebitis and inflammatory aggregates in the vitreous, described as a string of pearls, can be seen in sarcoidosis. The other autoimmune etiologies are diagnoses of exclusion. Infection should be ruled out before treating empirically with corticosteroids (choice C). WNV, detected with serologic testing for antiviral antibodies (choice D), is a single-stranded RNA flavivirus transmitted byCulexgenus mosquitoes. Approximately 70% to 80% of human WNV infections are subclinical. Most symptomatic cases present with acute fever, headache, weakness, myalgia, arthralgia, gastrointestinal upset, and/or transient maculopapular rash. Less than 1% of cases exhibit neuroinvasive disease. The most common ocular complication is multifocal chorioretinitis, but cranial nerve palsy, nystagmus, optic neuritis, retinal vasculitis, and anterior uveitis have been reported. Age greater than 45 years and diabetes are risk factors for WNV chorioretinitis.4 In neuroinvasive disease, CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis. However, neutrophils predominate early, are rapidly recruited to the site of WNV infection in mice, and support viral replication.5 MRI may show abnormalities in the basal ganglia, thalamus, and brainstem in patients with encephalitis. Fundus photos and retina OCT typically show a linear chorioretinitis due to spread along the retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL).6WNV can spread hematogenously via the choroid or neurally from the central nervous system to the RNFL, which may explain the combination of scattered and linear lesion formations in this patient. The patient’s symptoms and vitritis resolved with observation, while chorioretinal lesions persisted (Figure 2).

Ocular toxoplasmosis classically presents with vitritis overlying focal retinitis (ie, a headlight in the fog). Active toxoplasmosis is unlikely without retinitis (choice A). However, typically there are also anterior segment findings, like keratitis or iridocyclitis in onchocerciasis. Ocular cysticercosis can cause intracranial calcifications. Toxocara and other nematodes can cause subretinal tracks with diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis (DUSN), consistent with linear chorioretinal lesions. However, serologic and stool studies and peripheral blood smears are of little utility in helminthic infections (choice B).1Stool ova and parasite testing is low yield for toxocara, because ingested eggs cause an eosinophilic granulomatous immune reaction incompatible with helminth survival.2Although multiple toxocariasis phenotypes have been described, including DUSN and diffuse chorioretinal inflammation, the most common presentation is unilateral pediatric subretinal peripheral or posterior pole granulomas with clear media. Rheumatoid factor, which can cause false-positive WNV serology, was negative. The differential diagnosis for multifocal chorioretinitis includes nonhelminthic infectious causes, such as presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (POHS), and infectious causes, such as syphilis, tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis, pneumocystis choroiditis, and WNV. Although vitritis makes POHS much less likely, 5% of POHS patients, as a subset of multifocal choroiditis, have a linear streak of histoplasmosis spots parallel to the equator (ie, Schlaegel lines). Ocular toxoplasmosis classically presents with vitritis overlying focal retinitis (ie, a headlight in the fog). Active toxoplasmosis is unlikely without retinitis (choice A). The remaining etiologies are unlikely with negative serology and inconsistent imaging. Helminthic infections can cause chorioretinitis. However, typically there are also anterior segment findings, like keratitis or iridocyclitis in onchocerciasis. Ocular cysticercosis can cause intracranial calcifications. Toxocara and other nematodes can cause subretinal tracks with diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis (DUSN), consistent with linear chorioretinal lesions. However, serologic and stool studies and peripheral blood smears are of little utility in helminthic infections (choice B).1Stool ova and parasite testing is low yield for toxocara, because ingested eggs cause an eosinophilic granulomatous immune reaction incompatible with helminth survival.2Although multiple toxocariasis phenotypes have been described, including DUSN and diffuse chorioretinal inflammation, the most common presentation is unilateral pediatric subretinal peripheral or posterior pole granulomas with clear media. Adult ocular toxocariasis is exceedingly rare and usually presents with vitritis overlying a hazy white granuloma.3 Noninfectious causes include sarcoidosis, punctate inner choroidopathy, birdshot retinochoroidopathy, idiopathic multifocal choroiditis, and multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis. Linear periphlebitis and inflammatory aggregates in the vitreous, described as a string of pearls, can be seen in sarcoidosis. The other autoimmune etiologies are diagnoses of exclusion. Infection should be ruled out before treating empirically with corticosteroids (choice C). WNV, detected with serologic testing for antiviral antibodies (choice D), is a single-stranded RNA flavivirus transmitted byCulexgenus mosquitoes. Approximately 70% to 80% of human WNV infections are subclinical. Most symptomatic cases present with acute fever, headache, weakness, myalgia, arthralgia, gastrointestinal upset, and/or transient maculopapular rash. Less than 1% of cases exhibit neuroinvasive disease. The most common ocular complication is multifocal chorioretinitis, but cranial nerve palsy, nystagmus, optic neuritis, retinal vasculitis, and anterior uveitis have been reported. Age greater than 45 years and diabetes are risk factors for WNV chorioretinitis.4 In neuroinvasive disease, CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis. However, neutrophils predominate early, are rapidly recruited to the site of WNV infection in mice, and support viral replication.5 MRI may show abnormalities in the basal ganglia, thalamus, and brainstem in patients with encephalitis. Fundus photos and retina OCT typically show a linear chorioretinitis due to spread along the retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL).6WNV can spread hematogenously via the choroid or neurally from the central nervous system to the RNFL, which may explain the combination of scattered and linear lesion formations in this patient.
